---
title: "SupBioTech M2 (Paris): single-cell RNA-seq"
subtitle: "From a count matrix to cell types, sub-states, trajectories and gene sets"
---

**Audience:** M2 students, SupBioTech (Paris). **Data:** scRNA-seq ([GSE241132](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE241132)) of one donor (PWH27) at four timepoints: healthy skin and wounds at day 1, day 7 and day 30.

::: {.callout-important}
## The notebook
[**Open the practical notebook (web version)**](notebooks/Analysis_sc_students.ipynb), or download it to work on it: [`Analysis_sc_students.ipynb`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sarnatas/skinwound/main/supbiotech-m2/notebooks/Analysis_sc_students.ipynb) (right-click, *save link as*). It is a single file, with no helper module to install.

The web version shows the instructions, the empty cells and the folded hints, but **no results**: the figures appear when *you* run your own analysis.
:::

## What you will do

The notebook has **two halves**, which can be done in two sessions.

**First half (Parts 1-16): the whole tissue.**

1. Understand what a scRNA-seq count matrix is and what an `AnnData` object contains.
2. Quality control of cells and genes, doublet removal.
3. Normalisation, highly variable genes, PCA, neighbour graph and UMAP.
4. Think about **batch effects**, and when *not* to correct them.
5. Clustering (and how to choose the resolution), marker genes, **cell type annotation**, validation against the published annotation.
6. How the tissue composition changes during healing.

**Second half (Parts 17-21): zooming in on the keratinocytes.**

7. **Sub-clustering**: which states exist *inside* a cell type, and is the timepoint a biological or a technical effect?
8. **Trajectory and pseudotime** (PAGA, diffusion pseudotime): do the states form an ordered path, and which genes change along it?
9. **Gene set enrichment** (GSEA on a ranking of all genes): which biological processes change after wounding, and what are the traps (redundant terms, one donor)?

## How we work

Every section follows the same rhythm: a **Concept** to read, a code cell to **Run**, sometimes an experiment where we **Break it** on purpose, a **Question** whose answer is folded, and a **Take-home**. The notebook has three kinds of code cells (the coloured border is visible on the web version):

- <span class="legend-run">Run</span>: the code is already written. Execute it, then *look at the output*.
- <span class="legend-read">Read</span>: technical code already written (workarounds, plumbing). Execute it and read it carefully.
- <span class="legend-turn">Your turn</span>: an **empty cell** with a starter comment. **You write the code.**

Below each *Your turn* cell there are two folded boxes, to open **in this order and only after a real attempt**: **Hint 1** (the idea: which function, what its arguments mean) and **Hint 2** (the full solution, to run and then modify, not to copy blindly). Write your **choices and reasons** in the notes cells: they matter more than the code.

**What you hand in.** At the end of the course each student delivers **their own notebook** (one per student, even if you worked in a group): run from top to bottom, saved with its figures, with commented code and **a lot of text** that explains and justifies every step. The notebook *is* the report, there is no separate document. The details are in the section *Deliverable* at the end of the notebook.

## Setup

You will work **on your own computer** (Windows, Mac or Linux). All the software used here is **free and open source**. Follow the steps **in order**, and read each step to the end before typing anything.

::: {.callout-note}
## What you need
- A computer with **8 GB of RAM** at least (16 GB is comfortable) and **about 15 GB of free disk space**.
- An **internet connection**: for the installation (several GB are downloaded), and once more during the practical (Part 20).
- Some time for the installation, which is mostly waiting for downloads: **do it before the first session**, not during it.
:::

### Step 0 · One working folder, and the golden rule about paths

Create **one folder** for the whole course, for instance `supbiotech` in your home folder. Everything goes in it: `environment.yml`, the notebook, the `DATA` folder, and later your results.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Paths: pay attention, always
A **path** is the exact address of a file or a folder. The computer does not guess: if the path in the notebook is not exactly where the data are on **your** machine, nothing works (`FileNotFoundError`). Most of the problems of the first session come from here.

- Use a **short path without spaces, accents or special characters** (`C:/Users/anna/supbiotech` is good, `C:/Users/Anaïs Dupont/Université/mon cours` is asking for trouble).
- On Windows, **avoid folders synchronised by OneDrive** (very often *Desktop* and *Documents*): files can be "online only" and then are not really on your disk. Make the folder directly in your user folder.
- Write **full paths**, from the root of the disk. `~` and relative paths such as `../DATA` are an invitation to errors.
- To find the path of a folder: **Mac**: in Finder, right-click the folder, hold the `Option` key and choose *Copy "DATA" as Pathname*. **Windows**: hold `Shift`, right-click the folder, choose *Copy as path* (then replace every `\` by `/`, and remove the quotes if you add your own). **Linux**: open a terminal in the folder and type `pwd`.
:::

### Step 1 · Install conda (Miniforge)

**conda** is a program that installs software, and keeps each project in its own isolated "environment", so that nothing conflicts. We use **Miniforge**, the free and open source installer of conda (it takes its packages from the community channel *conda-forge*). Pick your system:

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### Windows

1. Download the installer: [`Miniforge3-Windows-x86_64.exe`](https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-Windows-x86_64.exe).
2. Double-click it. If Windows shows a blue "protected your PC" window, click *More info*, then *Run anyway*.
3. Accept the default choices (install for *Just Me*, keep *Create start menu shortcuts*).
4. When it is over, open the **Start menu** and type **Miniforge Prompt**: open it. It is a window with a black (or dark) background where you type commands. **From now on, always use this window, not PowerShell and not "Command Prompt"**.
5. Test it: type `conda --version` and press Enter. You should see something like `conda 25.x.x`.

#### Mac

1. Find out which kind of Mac you have: Apple menu → *About This Mac*. If you read **Chip: Apple M1 / M2 / M3 / M4**, all is well. If you read **Processor: Intel**, see the warning below.
2. Open the **Terminal** (press `Cmd + Space`, type *Terminal*, Enter).
3. Copy and paste these two lines, one at a time, pressing Enter after each:

   ```
   curl -L -O "https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-$(uname)-$(uname -m).sh"
   bash Miniforge3-$(uname)-$(uname -m).sh
   ```
4. The installer asks questions. Press Enter to read the licence (press the space bar to scroll down), type `yes` to accept, press Enter to accept the proposed location, and answer `yes` when it asks whether to initialise conda.
5. **Close the Terminal and open a new one.** The line now starts with `(base)`: conda is active. Test it: type `conda --version`.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Mac with an Intel processor
With the software versions of this course, the environment of Step 2 **cannot be installed** on a Mac with an Intel processor (some packages are not available for it). Do not lose time: ask the instructor, and read the last section of this page (working in a group).
:::

#### Linux

1. Open a terminal.
2. Copy and paste these two lines, one at a time, pressing Enter after each (if `wget` is missing: `sudo apt install wget`, or use `curl -L -O` instead):

   ```
   wget "https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-$(uname)-$(uname -m).sh"
   bash Miniforge3-$(uname)-$(uname -m).sh
   ```
3. Press Enter to read the licence (space bar to scroll), type `yes` to accept, press Enter to accept the proposed location, and answer `yes` when it asks whether to initialise conda.
4. **Close the terminal and open a new one.** The line now starts with `(base)`. Test it: `conda --version`.

:::

### Step 2 · Create the Python environment

1. Download the two files of the course into your working folder (right-click on the link, *Save link as*; **check that the names end exactly in `.yml` and `.ipynb`**, Windows sometimes adds `.txt`):
   - [`environment.yml`](environment.yml) (the list of the software to install);
   - [`Analysis_sc_students.ipynb`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sarnatas/skinwound/main/supbiotech-m2/notebooks/Analysis_sc_students.ipynb) (the notebook).
2. In your terminal (**Miniforge Prompt** on Windows), go to the working folder with `cd`, then check that the file is there (replace `anna` and the folder name with yours). You must see `environment.yml` in the list.

   Windows (Miniforge Prompt):

   ```
   cd C:\Users\anna\supbiotech
   dir
   ```

   Mac / Linux (Terminal):

   ```
   cd ~/supbiotech
   ls
   ```

3. Create the environment, activate it, and register it as a Jupyter kernel:

   ```
   conda env create -f environment.yml
   conda activate supbiotech-sc
   python -m ipykernel install --user --name skinwound --display-name "Python (skinwound)"
   ```

   - The first command takes **a long time** (10 to 30 minutes, depending on your connection) and prints a lot of text: this is normal. Wait until you get your prompt back without an error.
   - After the second command, the line starts with **`(supbiotech-sc)`**: the environment is active.
   - The third command makes the environment visible to Jupyter, under the name *Python (skinwound)*.
4. Quick test (still in the same terminal):

   ```
   python -c "import scanpy; print(scanpy.__version__)"
   ```

   It should print `1.11.5`.

If the installation stops with an error, copy the **last lines** of the message and send them to the instructor. Before trying again, remove the half-built environment: `conda env remove -n supbiotech-sc`.

### Step 3 · Download and unzip the data

1. Download the archive **`DATA.zip`** (about 300 MB) from this link: [**download DATA.zip**](https://filesender.renater.fr/?s=download&token=0623510d-08a4-4fe4-a59f-491a384215a1). (The page may ask you to accept the terms; the link is valid **until Tuesday 20 October 2026**: after that date, ask the instructor.)
2. Put `DATA.zip` in your working folder (the same as before).
3. **Unzip** it. Pick your system:

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### Windows

*Option A (recommended): from the Miniforge Prompt*, in your working folder:

```
tar -xf DATA.zip
```

*Option B: with the mouse.* Right-click `DATA.zip`, then *Extract All...*. **Pay attention**: the window proposes a destination that ends with `\DATA`. **Delete this last `\DATA`** from the destination, so that it ends with your working folder (`...\supbiotech`), then click *Extract*. If you do not, you get `DATA\DATA` (a folder inside a folder) and the paths will be wrong. (If *Extract All* does not work, the free and open source program [7-Zip](https://www.7-zip.org/) does the job.)

#### Mac

Double-click `DATA.zip` in the Finder: a folder `DATA` appears next to it. Or, in the Terminal, from your working folder:

```
unzip DATA.zip
```

#### Linux

In a terminal, from your working folder (if `unzip` is missing: `sudo apt install unzip`):

```
unzip DATA.zip
```

Or right-click the file in your file manager and choose *Extract Here*.

:::

4. **Check the result.** Your working folder must look like this (a folder `__MACOSX` may also appear: ignore it, or delete it; **do not unzip the `.gz` files** inside the sample folders, the software reads them as they are):

   ```
   supbiotech/
   ├── environment.yml
   ├── Analysis_sc_students.ipynb
   └── DATA/
       ├── PWH27D0/                    one folder per sample (healthy skin)
       │   ├── matrix.mtx.gz           the counts
       │   ├── barcodes.tsv.gz         the names of the cells
       │   └── features.tsv.gz         the names of the genes
       ├── PWH27D1/                    the same, wound at day 1
       ├── PWH27D7/                    the same, wound at day 7
       ├── PWH27D30/                   the same, wound at day 30
       ├── GSE241132_cell_metadata.txt the annotation published by the authors
       └── paper_marker_genes.csv      marker genes reported in the paper
   ```

   Check with `ls DATA` (Mac / Linux) or `dir DATA` (Windows): you must see `PWH27D0`, `PWH27D1`, `PWH27D7`, `PWH27D30`, `GSE241132_cell_metadata.txt` and `paper_marker_genes.csv` **directly**. If you only see another folder called `DATA`, you have a folder inside a folder: move its content one level up.

**This is everything the analysis needs.** There is nothing else to download by hand: the folder for your results (`my_results`) is created by the notebook, and the Gene Ontology library of Part 20 is downloaded automatically, once.

The raw data are public on GEO ([GSE241132](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE241132)); the archive contains only the four samples of the donor used in the course.

### Step 4 · Start JupyterLab and open the notebook

In the terminal (Miniforge Prompt on Windows), activate the environment, go to the working folder and start JupyterLab:

```
conda activate supbiotech-sc
cd <your working folder>
jupyter lab
```

A tab opens in your web browser (if not, copy the address starting with `http://localhost:8888/...` that appears in the terminal into the browser). In the file list on the left, double-click `Analysis_sc_students.ipynb`. At the top right of the notebook the kernel must be **Python (skinwound)**; if it is not, use the menu *Kernel → Change Kernel...* and choose it.

- **Leave the terminal open** while you work: it is the program running JupyterLab. To stop everything at the end, save the notebook, then press `Ctrl + C` twice in the terminal.
- **Next times, you only repeat Step 4.** Steps 1 to 3 are done once.

### Step 5 · Tell the notebook where things are

In the notebook, the first code cell (Part 1, *Setup*) has two lines to edit, `DATA` and `OUT`. Write the **full path** of your `DATA` folder and of a folder for your results (it will be created if it does not exist), between quotes:

| System | `DATA` | `OUT` |
|---|---|---|
| Windows | `"C:/Users/anna/supbiotech/DATA"` | `"C:/Users/anna/supbiotech/my_results"` |
| Mac | `"/Users/anna/supbiotech/DATA"` | `"/Users/anna/supbiotech/my_results"` |
| Linux | `"/home/anna/supbiotech/DATA"` | `"/home/anna/supbiotech/my_results"` |

On **Windows, write the slashes as `/`**, not `\`: in Python, `\` has a special meaning and `"C:\Users\anna"` gives an error.

Run the cell (`Shift + Enter`). If the path is right it prints **`Data found: OK`**. If it prints a `FileNotFoundError`, the message tells you which file was not found: fix the path (compare it character by character with the path you copied in Step 0) and run the cell again. **Do not go on until you see `Data found: OK`.**

Now you can start: read the notebook from the top.

## Tips

- **Memory.** The first half needs about 8 GB of RAM for this donor (16 GB is comfortable). If the kernel dies ("the kernel appears to have died"), typically at the doublet step, close the other programs (browser tabs, etc.) before anything else.
- **Disk.** The notebook saves checkpoints of your analysis in `OUT` (several files of about 1 GB each). Keep an eye on your free disk space.
- Run the cells **in order**, and read the error message (its last line first) before asking for help. *Kernel → Restart Kernel and Run All Cells* tells you whether your notebook works from scratch; cells that depend on a *Your turn* cell you have not completed yet will fail: that is expected.
- **Cluster numbers are not stable** from one computer to another: the same group of cells can get a different number. Always check the marker genes, not only the number.
- **Paths, again.** A `FileNotFoundError` almost always means a wrong path: check `DATA` and `OUT` first.
- The first run of Part 20 downloads the Gene Ontology library (internet needed, only once); afterwards it is read from the local cache in `OUT`.
- Whenever you pick a threshold or a parameter, be ready to justify it with a plot.

### Common problems

- **`conda` is not recognised / `command not found`.** On Windows, you are not in the *Miniforge Prompt*. On Mac / Linux, you did not close and reopen the terminal after the installation.
- **The environment is not active** (the line does not start with `(supbiotech-sc)`). Type `conda activate supbiotech-sc`.
- **The kernel *Python (skinwound)* is not in the list.** Activate the environment and type again the third command of Step 2 (`python -m ipykernel install ...`), then reload the browser page.
- **`ModuleNotFoundError`** (for instance `No module named 'scanpy'`). The notebook is running with the wrong kernel: choose *Python (skinwound)* (Step 4).
- **`FileNotFoundError`.** A wrong path: see Step 5.

## If you cannot make it work

**It is not a problem if you do not manage to install everything.** Computers, networks and operating systems are all different, and installing scientific software is sometimes difficult even for professionals.

1. **First, ask me**, the instructor: send me the last lines of the error message (copy and paste text rather than a photo, if you can). Many problems are solved in a few minutes.
2. **Working in small groups of 2, 3 or 4 people is fully accepted, and even recommended**, using a computer where everything works. Choose the machine that has the installation working and a screen big enough for everyone; take turns at the keyboard, and everybody writes, discusses and understands. Discussing the choices (thresholds, resolution, cell type names...) is at least as valuable as typing the code.
